english_verification.review_scope: Read the actual formation-decision excerpt, Warlord Empire reform/Vainglory mission effect, and current English flavour passages about Taychendi views of the Exemplars and imperial apotheosis. The public display name is Taychendi Empire; Effelai is the native English region spelling. Read the two actual fixed-revision regional/timeline chunks. The Wiki material provides related regional and predecessor history, not an independent J84 country history. No predecessor-tree audit or mission recount was performed. Primary compared all native idea names/descriptions by actual current English localisation key. Source ranges may be locator envelopes; conditional and predecessor idea sets remain separate. No formal validators, tests, builds or browser checks were run.
unresolved: No dedicated J84 Wiki country page was found; ancient unifications and the warlord cycle remain regional setting background, not proof of Tag continuity.
J84's 1057 historical-scenario ruler is not a 1444 starting ruler.
The exact late-campaign sequence varies with predecessor and conditional branches; no exhaustive route audit was performed.

rationale.campaign_length: The J84 main file has 54 direct missions, with some predecessor missions continuing according to the campaign's origin; 212 linked mission entities are not a single-campaign total.
rationale.colonization: Directions into Chendhya, the Effelai, and Amadia involve distant settlement, development, and colonial-style conquest.
rationale.complexity: Predecessor mission inheritance, religious reform, Vainglory, the warlord system, and multi-region expeditions all add complexity.
rationale.dark_story: Enslaved mining, plunder, suppression choices, and world-spanning hegemony are major parts of the text.
rationale.difficulty: The main challenge comes from a high-pressure Taychendi prelude followed by multi-front expansion and governance after formation.
rationale.diplomacy: Relations with predecessor subjects and imperial frontiers require management, though forceful expansion remains the primary solution.
rationale.early_pressure: Competition in the Taychendi prelude is intense: subjects, aggressive expansion, and religious reform must be managed together.
rationale.magic_artifice_intensity: Hero worship, Precursor relics, artifice, and the search for a flying city run through the middle and late campaign.
rationale.narrative_density: The warlord cycle, dynastic apotheosis, frontier conquests, and lost flying city make a long, connected story.
rationale.tall_play: Cities, farms, temples, monuments, and artifice matter, but this is not an inward-looking tall campaign.
rationale.trade_economy: Vainglory and warlord plunder are invested in cities, agriculture, mining, and commercial networks.
rationale.warfare: Unifying Taychend and conquering beyond it drive nearly every main storyline.

identity.appearance: Does not exist in 1444. Formable by decision after reforming the Taychendi Pantheon and meeting regional development, stability, and peace requirements; occupying all of Taychend is not required.

predecessors.relationship: Can form J84 and retain predecessor missions that are available only to a J84 that was formerly G64.

national_ideas.scope_note: National traditions, seven national ideas and ambition only; optional idea groups and racial/government bonuses are excluded. Conditional alternatives are separate, not stacked. Adopting new ideas depends on the actual event/decision and player choice.

description.text:
Ebenanth, Yodhan, Ultarlanbeg, Olhokar. These rulers conquered Taychend, only for their empires to crumble after their demise. The Nakari and Gophirans also conquered Taychend, and attempted to build a longer lasting empire… but in the end, they failed as well.

This is all in the past now, for Taychend is once again united under our rule. One thing is certain, however: we must not let history repeat. We stand on the shoulders of giants, whose achievements and failures shaped our present reality, and while all those that came before us failed to build a truly unified Taychend, they will serve as a lesson for our emperors and scholars.

Every mistake our forebears made will be studied in detail, every folly analyzed, every success investigated, and every achievement outdone.

description.text:
Our faith in the divinity of ascended heroes has created an issue now that there is no more endemic warfare in Taychend. The easiest way for a common peasant to ascend, through combat and bravery, has been closed to them. For most this is a cause for celebration. But those with ambition will see their opportunities to ascend dwindling before their very eyes.

Thus, we have set out a new program to encourage the pursuits of less warlike occupations that give our more ambitious citizens the opportunity to become gods. Most notably, this program has led to an increase in intellectual pursuits, even among the lower classes.

description.text:
Ever since the ruin of Aelantir, Taychend has known nothing but warfare and chaos. For millennia and beyond, the most common way a farmer could meet his end was either on the field of battle or at the edge of a marauding soldier’s blade.

With the end of unavailing warfare came a population explosion. As new generations were raised in peace and prosperity, as new crops and farming techniques spread to Taychend by way of Cannorian traders and experts, the population boomed and grew to heights never before seen in Taychend.

description.text: Taychend’s enormous population led to a massive excess of recruits, something high-ranking commanders quickly realised and exploited. They morphed the imperial doctrine to fit this new reality, and millions of young warriors voluntarily joined the army to be sent as garrisons or to fight upon the frontiers against the barbarians. Whenever outsiders dared to try to attack the empire, a quick mobilization of hundreds of thousands of soldiers was all it took for them to leave.

description.text:
During the waning days of the 2nd Gophiran Empire, a philosopher named Tailatam wrote a series of books detailing his thoughts on how the Taychendi empire of his day could best secure its future and end the warlord cycle. While he died before he ever saw his writings be applied to the real world, his writings would form the core of what became known as the "Tailatam System".

The Tailatam System was a form of governance practiced by the empire of Taychend. At the top of the hierarchy sits the emperor, who appoints provincial governors to the provinces. These governors can be removed at any time, and only have a term of 5 years. After every 5 years, these governors return to the capital either to be fired or to be assigned to a different province. During their meeting with the emperor, they must share bread and wine while showing utter loyalty, risking execution if they fail to do so.

Nobility was not heritable under the Tailatam system. All land was owned by the emperor, and was "rented out" to the aristocracy. Thus, the nobility were forced to stay loyal, obeying all orders of the emperor and the provincial governors. For if they disobeyed, they would lose their position immediately… along with their heads.

description.text: The task of ruling an empire the size of Taychend was no small feat; it could even be considered to be of legendary proportions. Thus it was no surprise to many that upon the death of the first emperor, they were declared a god. Subsequently, all emperors were declared gods upon death and, as their statues appeared in every city, the imperial cult became widespread. With this, the common people now felt they had a connection with the royal family. This not only reduced unrest in the empire, but also encouraged the loyalty of commoners towards the king and crown.

description.text:
In the 1600s, a new, smaller kind of outsider arrived on our shores, bringing with them strange magically powered inventions. Known as "artificery", many of our leaders were quick to see this technology’s potential, especially with all the ancient, powerful relics found in Taychend. These relics, as it turned out, were very useful in the application of artificery, which was the reason these foreigners came to our land to begin with.

It was decided to invite more of these "artificers" to come to our land, where they could practice and innovate upon their inventions freely and openly, away from the watchful gaze of the Ravelian Church and the Gommo. Their only concession was that they must share with us any and all artificer inventions useful for warfare. They either agreed to our terms or were promptly returned to where they had originally fled from.

description.text:
When the skies turned dark, many fled to the fortified manors of the ancient lords past, who then used the refugees for their own benefit. In one such manor a city grew, built on a defensible cliffside and ruled over by a tyrannical lord. He forced the refugees to slave away in the gold mines of the area, for that was but the only way they could receive the food and water which the tyrant controlled.

Merialeth was one such slave who, with a band of followers, escaped into the dangerous countryside. They built up their forces, and, on one stormy night, snuck into the mansion. They sneakily took out every guard in their way, managing to reach the tyrant’s bedside unhindered. Merialeth beheaded the tyrant with a special magic blade, ending his reign.

The next day, she was proclaimed the first queen of Urvand. She freed all the slaves, earning for herself the title "The Manumitter", and set about organizing Urvand into a proper city. After 22 years of rule, she left this world, bequeathing the city to her successors. Every petty noble of Urvand claims descent from the legendary queen, but only a true descendant of Merialeth can rule Urvand.

description.text: The Larankarha horse is stronger, tougher, and stockier than its Taychendi contemporaries. While every Larankarha city has their own special breed of Larankarha horse, Urvand’s is noted for not being particularly unique. Instead, Urvand focused on breeding and sustaining massive populations of these horses, such that entire armies of Urvand’s warriors would ride into battle on the saddle. Urvand developed a specialized logistics corps, whose primary duty was not to fight, but to supply everything these horse riders required.

description.text: When Urvand consolidated the lands of the Larankarha, it propagated a simple but effective message: Urvand is the ultimate and final kingdom of the Larankarha, and anyone that opposes this will be crushed. This was the core ideology Urvand’s rulers followed, and they even went so far as to rename their state to Larankar to better reflect this unifying ideology. As Urvand subjugated the rest of the Larankarha over the 15th century, it replaced local rulers with puppets that followed this same ideology, while cunningly using propaganda to slowly wither away the local identities of the original Larankarha.

description.text:
"I started my rule with Urvand full of ramshackle tents and decaying structures, but left it an organized city built of stone and gold."
- the final words of Merialeth

One of the core goals every ruler of Urvand must follow is to improve their city, in so doing following the will of Merialeth. The core powerbase of the monarch are the citizens of Urvand, who will gladly stay loyal as long as their city is invested in. Thus, the city of Urvand is a beauty full of gold and opulence, resting upon and expanding into the cliffside. On the other hand, the opulent gold is mined by slaves and criminals, whose labor is used to build the city of Urvand; the forever expanding city holds this sordid secret deep within.

description.text:
From the moment Erankar took breath he defied the odds, cut free from his mother and taken by fever as a newborn. Be it his daring escape from the hands of Enlarmai after the fall of his city and the execution of his family, his tortuous years spent in the Larankarha wilderness hunting with his bare hands just to survive, the half a decade he spent working his way towards one of the fiercest mercenary bands in Taychend, or his incredible and crushing victory over Enlarmai and the resulting utter destruction of their capital. At every moment, in every crisis, Erankar the Defiant spat in the face of fate, and won.

It was this defiance – this unceasing determination and unbreakable will – that allowed Erankar to create the largest state the Larankarha had ever seen. And at the Battle of Masialendi, when it was thought that no one could even harm Laskaris the Conqueror - let alone kill him - it was this defiance that allowed Erankar to land a near mortal blow on the invader, routing his army, and saving Taychend from total Kheionai dominance. No matter the challenge Larankar faces, the descendants of Erankar will always remember the spirit of the Defiant and fight against the judgements of fate for their people’s ascendency.

description.text:
As outsiders march upon Taychend, many warlords fall and the people suffer, as seemingly no one can stand against them. Yet, there is one kingdom that has proven itself able to resist the foreigners: Larankar. From Erankar almost killing the seemingly invincible Laskaris, to the resistance against the Sun Elves, every Taychendi seeking to liberate their homeland knows who to turn to.

These exiled warriors who fled to Larankar joined the kingdom’s army. Known as the Hadas Katti, Blades of Despair, they helped bolster the numbers of Larankar’s armies, aiding in the kingdom’s survival in the centuries to come.

description.text:
It is said that when Erankar visited a local oracle during his march through Kalavend, the oracle spoke of how Erankar’s realm would meet its end "under the coming of the eastern sun". Erankar, an elf infamous for his defiance and disregard of fate, dismissed this as pointless, for the sun already rose in the east.

In 1516, the Jaherian Exemplars landed in South Aelantir, planning to march into Taychend and spread the truth of Surael. They found an environment ripe for disruption, as the current king of Larankar, a descendant of Erankar the Defiant, had fallen ill and was incapable of ruling. Using this brief period of weakness, the subjugated lords of Kalavend allied themselves with the Sun Elves, and launched an uprising against Larankar.

As the Kalavendhi-Exemplar alliance marched to Urvand, Larankar’s armies resisted fiercely. The siege of Urvand lasted a year, with the Sun Elves taking the city, freeing its slaves, and razing the capital. Larankar’s empire had fallen. Yet not all hope was lost, as the alliance quickly turned on each other, giving Urvand the respite it needed to rebuild. A century passed, but eventually Urvand persevered, and could shine once more.

description.text:
When the world ended, and Taychend was reduced to a mess of bandits and tyrannical warlords, there were scarce few places of safety for those already at the bottom of pre-Ruin society. One of these lights in the darkness was Gophira, "the Fort". Led ably by Bukka Raya, called the Greenbringer for his use of magic to grow food through the harshest winters, the people of Gophira constructed great fortifications to protect the fledgling haven from the assaults of those who would seek to loot or destroy it.

Nowadays, the legacy of the Greenbringer is clear – Gophira stands as the greatest fort in Taychend, its fortifications upgraded and expanded over time. Though the scars of battle linger on the stones of the great fortress, and the citadel has not escaped conquest or subjugation entirely, the rows of cyclopean walls and piercing towers stand as a testament to the greatest lesson the Gophirans learnt from their founder-god: complacency in defence is a fatal weakness.

description.text:
At the heart of Taychend lie the Iron Hills, an area of jagged peaks, heavily forested river valleys and, as the name suggests, an incredible amount of iron. Each of the three "Iron Cities" of the hills prides themselves on different specialties – while Banderuttai strive to improve their stalwart shields and fearsome armour, and Kattisangamar are ever-willing to brandish their fine sabres and swords, Gophira’s pride is their sheer productive capability. From the days of Bukka Raya to the apex of the Second Gophiran Empire, the foundries and smithies of Gophira have worked tirelessly to produce every manner of iron or steel object needed for the city’s needs.

Perhaps it is this industrious flexibility that has allowed Gophira to dominate its two brother cities for so long. While recent misfortunes have allowed them to reclaim their independence, the Kings of Gophira know that should they ever bring Kattisangamar and Banderuttai to heel again, they will once again stand as the undisputed Iron Masters of Yodhanpir.

description.text:
When the Chendhyan King of Kings, Ultarlanbeg the Decimator, invaded Taychend, he swept aside all who stood against him. Even after he was assassinated by a Taychendi concubine, his son Geladhlan ruthlessly suppressed the mass native revolt that erupted. Long past the fall of the Asezhudar, many feared that Taychend might forever be subjected to Chendhyan rule, as a dozen remnant "Aedzudars" were carved from the lands of the old Empire. Then Olhokar rose, and they feared no longer.

Giving himself entirely to the hands of fate, at every turn Olhokar consulted oracles and diviners, and from his powerbase in Gophira, recently refortified after its sacking by Ultarlanbeg, Olhokar conducted an incredible campaign against the Chendhyan Aedzudars. With fate by his side, he restored native rule to Taychend, and in doing so became the first native emperor of Taychend in over 500 years.

Alas, his reign would be brief – in service to the dark words of an oracle, Olhokar sacrificed his eldest child to secure Gophira’s future, provoking a massive revolt that shattered his realm. However, even this would prove fortuitous for Olhokar’s beloved city, as the line of his second son would themselves piece back together the empire the Fortuitous first conquered.

description.text:
After the collapse of the First Gophiran Empire, the now greatly reduced Gophira was forced to fight several costly wars in order to save what remained of its territory. While for a time it seemed that Gophira would be drowned in the tide of fate, drastic times called for drastic measures. Harrihara IV created the "Ironblood Army", a military class drawn from both the cities and countryside, with mandated training and heavily subsidised equipment. Able to be called up at a moment’s notice, Gophira created a large and dependable core of infantry, whose constant readiness allowed them to maintain their martial traditions. While expensive, this would give Gophira the edge they needed over the city’s enemies.

As this force broke Oremvand’s Chendhyan mercenaries in the Oremvandian Wars, and reconquered the territory Gophira had lost, the military of the Sangamars once again transformed. Funded using the heavy taxes levied on the their many subject cities, the Ironblood Army would become a truly professional force during the Second Empire, crushing countless revolts and warlord-pretenders. While this professionalism would eventually be Gophira’s downfall, their legacy is nonetheless one of martial excellence and incredible capability.

description.text:
Gophira ruled over all Taychend for nearly a hundred years, and though the empire is primarily remembered for its military might, nowhere else is the legacy of their greatness more clear than in Kannalulthe, the Great Dam City. Founded originally as a simple fort guarding the river that leads to Gophira, as the Second Gophiran Empire expanded, Kannalulthe quickly became the centre of the Taychendi economy. Wishing to be close to the centre of Imperial power, merchant houses, slave traders, metalworkers and all other sorts of industries moved to the city. Soon enough, Kannalulthe became the de facto imperial capital, further expanding until it outgrew even Nanru Nakar in size and population.

While Kannalulthe fell far after the end of the Second Gophiran Empire, even now the ruins are vast and magnificent. The city’s cyclopean arches and walls, monumental temples, shrines and statues, and of course the eponymous dam that dominates the centre of the city, all continue to inspire the architects of Gophira – not to mention the incredible quantity of building materials that can be found within the city’s ruins. In this way, the legacy of Kannalulthe can be seen across the Gophira of today.

description.text:
It was in the military that the seeds of the Second Empire’s downfall were sowed – as the army became increasingly professional, it also became more political and independent, a process that culminated in its use by Celepana the Usurper to seize power from her brother, her father’s chosen heir. The resulting battle of Nymbhava, that saw the Ironblood Army split and arrayed against itself, was one of the largest battles in Taychendi history. Nymbhava would eventually prove to be the inciting incident for the terrible drama that would consume the Empire, setting in motion a chain of events that would lead to the War of the Six Emperors.

For nearly 15 years, Gophira fell into a vicious cycle of rebellion and mutinies that eventually caused its violent disintegration. However, this period of ceaseless warfare also saw some of the greatest military feats of the empire. With both Ironblood soldiers and Sangamar pretenders faced with utter destruction, Gophiran military excellence returned in stunning fashion, and the legacy of the tactics and great deeds in those wars inspire the men of Gophira even today.

description.text:
Though Gophira eventually fell to the same forces of pride and ambition that had claimed the empires of Ebenanth, the Mudaliars and even Ultarlanbeg, at its peak Gophira managed to soar to heights never before reached. Ruling with unprecedented strength and authority, for a time it seemed they might have been able to subjugate entirely the centres of Taychendi civilisation, and end the curse of warlordism that had afflicted Taychend since the Ruin.

Though their empire fell, and the defeat of Dhalinar III by Laskaris the Conqueror in the early 15th century put an end to any hope of a third Gophiran resurgence, the people of the Fort know in their heart that their history is one to be proud of. They once possessed the last and greatest empire of Taychend – and they may yet conquer another.

description.text:
The Straight Road is a trade route as well-used as it is ancient. Cutting across southern Taychend east-west from Korrimadhala to Imarchend, the route has long been the south’s inland economic artery – though the Tenvacha portion of it was not always so integral. While the overland route up the Vyech to the Kalavend remained open, Vuls Tenvach was impoverished. But when the bandits of Sibisimra rose in the 400s and cut that road off, the merchants of the south had to find a different route to the Kalavend – through the sea, via Vuls Tenvach.

Vuls Tenvach took great advantage of this sudden change in the mercantile landscape. Building its strength over the 5th century, it carved a great empire along the entirety of the Straight Road during the 6th and 7th, breaking Sibisimra’s power in the process. Though their period of rule would come to an end when one of their generals, a certain Eletam the Gold, betrayed them and integrated the city into his new Dumrusvarn Dannuka, the Tenvacha remain proud of their history, and temples to the heroes that once mastered the Straight Road line the avenues of Vuls Tenvach.

description.text: The southern regions of Vuls Tenvach are famed around Taychend for producing the world’s most luxurious Tapheta cloth, a crisp fabric with a smooth feel, known for holding its shape extremely well. Before the founding of Ameion, this fame had driven merchants and caravans to our cities for many centuries – with the opening of the Path of Wine going west to the Kheionai, Tenvacha ports became even busier as the westerners sought Taychendi produced textiles. Tapheta would also become one of most sought after goods in Taychend for the Cannorians, whose women’s fashion especially had begun to emphasise the stiffness Tapheta provided. The massive increase in Tapheta’s price that occurred when Ameion closed their ports would be one of the main causes of the later Cannorian intervention and subsequent imposition of the Deylokem system.

description.text:
Invading Vuls Tenvach is more difficult than one would think. With the cities of the north protected by a river and strong fortifications, and the cities of the south shielded by the rugged hills of Uyarbaid, one must embark on a costly campaign of over-river sieges, or march south along the coast via Nagar Vyechei. Though a treaty with Laskaris prevented its conquest for decades, when war did break out Ameion chose the latter route. This southern campaign faced problems too, however – the storms of Cape Thekvussam are legendary, known for wrecking inexperienced captains trying to round the cape. Only the sailors of Vuls Tenvach were able to navigate it without issue, and resupply the cities of the south coast, preventing their capture.

Through precise planning and timing, the ruler of Vuls Tenvach, Alvardip Tailarudu, managed to lure the Ambhen navy into a sea storm off the cape, which obliterated most of the enemy fleet at minimal cost to his own and doomed Ameion’s campaign. The Kappadi War, or the War of the Navigators, would help preserve Tenvacha independence for another 60 years, and though he would die soon after, Alvardip Tailarudu would become a widely worshipped god-hero.

description.text:
A controversial figure, Olorises Pulojith was a bastard prince born to Alvardip Tailarudu and an Ambhen concubine, who would rule Vuls Tenvach from the 1470s to the early 1500s. Owing to his heritage, Olorises believed that Vuls Tenvach must adapt to the ways of the Kheionai to survive. Seeing his siblings as foolish for their traditionalism, Olorises staged a coup to usurp the throne from his half-sister, and soon set himself to reforming his kingdom along Ambhen lines. On land, Olorises pioneered the Tenvacha Phalanx, relentlessly drilling his troops in the unwieldy but powerful formation.

Despite his abrasive and stubborn personality alienating him from the ageing Emperor Erankar, his military reforms would prove their worth at the legendary Battle of Gena, where the Tenvacha pikemen would defeat Ameion’s own in a fair fight, driving them from the field in a stunning victory. Though a lack of Larankarha support meant Olorises was unable to decisively follow up on his successes, his many victories would earn Olorises the official designation by the Ambhen Synkletos as an “Enemy of Ameion” – a badge of honour for any Free Taychendi.

description.text:
As the Ambhen navy learnt from the lessons of Alvardip, and set its sights once more on gaining naval supremacy, Olorises Pulojith knew that he needed to find a new edge against Ameion – and in the Bag of Winds, he found it. Said to be powered by a captured air elemental, the legendary Bag of Winds could propel a single normal sized ship forwards at great speed – or, of course, propel a single colossal ship forwards when physics would otherwise prevent it.

Looking to the massive galleys of the Alecandi Kheions for inspiration, over 5 years Olorises built the Deyodéikakaupos, a warship so large it had 20 tiers of oars, required 8000 rowers to move, even with the support of the Bag of Winds, and was said to have a complement of 5000 archers and 5000 marines. No matter the exact numbers, the ship guaranteed Vuls Tenvach’s safety at sea. After Olorises’ death and the fall of Vuls Tenvach, it was seized by Ameion, serving as the flagship of their navy. Eventually, it would meet its end fighting a titanic battle against the Exemplars’ Diranhria, blown to pieces by its rival ship’s precursor weaponry – though not before its ram narrowly missed cleaving the Precursor warship in two.

description.text:
Though the reign of Olorises made Vuls Tenvach the third power in Taychend, independent from Larankar or Ameion, his success could not outlast his death. After the siege of Vuls Tenvach in the 1510s the Kingdom was first vassalised as an Ambhen protectorate, then, after a failed revolt in 1565, annexed. However, Vuls Tenvach – now Degíthion – would not be so easily integrated into Ameion’s empire.

As Olorises the Great had already spent considerable effort introducing Kheionai customs and administration into Tenvacha political life, there already existed a class of semi-Kheionised nobles and warlords, who clashed with the newly raised Klereyren, on top of the many Thekvrystana who maintained their traditional ways. The addition of the Oren Nayiru and eventually Ravelianism divided the coast further. Nonetheless, the province’s governors would attempt to solve the issue, even sponsoring a Thekvrystana colonial expedition to the Severed Coast in order to deport some of their more contentious Taychendi subjects.

description.text:
As Ameion’s rule frayed at the seams in the late 18th century, and Taychendi radicals and Ravelian missionaries once more found their way into Degíthion, the divided coast became ripe for revolution – and the spark that would finally blow up Ameion’s empire. Monarchist-Liberal Radicals, imprisoned by Ameion on the prison-isle of Baruanasi, joined with Thekvrystana colonists returning from the severed coast to overthrow Ambhen rule, starting the Degíthion War in 1787.

Kemnarius Laskaris, the latest in the line of distinguished generals belonging to the line of the Conqueror, was sent to crush them – but as he began making progress against the rebels, a series of misinterpreted messages would result in him betraying Ameion and declaring himself King of Degíthion, leading the rebels and his own forces against those Ameion sent to stop him. Eventually converting to Ravelianism to secure Cannorian support, Kemnarius would unite the divided coast under his charismatic leadership, turning Degíthion into the strongest of the states that seceded from Ameion in the late 1800s.

player_overview.avoid_if: For players who do not want a high-pressure Taychendi prelude or dislike slave mining, colonial plunder, and continued expansion in the late campaign.
player_overview.how_it_plays: First reform the religion with the chosen predecessor, expand in Taychend, and meet the formation threshold. As J84, consolidate the warlord system, build Vainglory, then expand abroad and develop cities, artifice, and relic research.
player_overview.overview: The Taychendi Empire is not a starting country; it is a long-formable campaign available after Taychendi states meet religious-reform and regional-development thresholds. You inherit some missions from your chosen predecessor, then enter the shared imperial arc: make warlords fight for the dynasty, turn conquest into development through Vainglory, reach toward the Kheionai, Chendhya, and Amadia, and pursue the Star-Sunderer and the lost flying city. It is a conquest campaign that grows in scale and darkness.
player_overview.recommended_for: Players who enjoy continuous wars, a very long formable-country arc, a resource power bar, ancient legacies, and a dark imperial story.
signature_features: The J84 main file has 54 direct missions; predecessor missions can continue according to former Tag, but all 212 linked definitions are not playable at once.
An early Warlord Empire mission unlocks Vainglory, tying spoils from war to agriculture, veteran settlement, and construction.
Imperial worship, artifice, and Precursor relics connect large-scale South Aelantir conquest to an endgame search for a flying city.
player_overview.tagline: Unite Taychend's warlords, forge victory into cities and artifice, then pursue a flying city and a new age.

reasons: The regional prelude varies by predecessor, while formation opens a vast shared imperial campaign.
Vainglory binds continuous warfare to national development in a distinctive gameplay loop.
Precursor relics, artifice, and the flying city give the late empire a clear narrative goal.
warnings: J84 is not a 1444 starting country; religious reform and formation requirements come first.
The figure 212 is the total of linked mission entities, not the playable mission count in one campaign.
The imperial storyline explicitly includes enslavement, plunder, and brutal colonial content.

positive_indicators: Development of local cities and agriculture.
values.rationale: War and hegemony are not treated as moral deductions in themselves, but slave mining, colonial plunder, and treating world-spanning war as an imperial mission remain clear problems for personhood and restraint.
